verdict: Caution on Srinagar tourism/hospitality lending: fund only cash-collateralised, working-capital lines to operators with verified footfall; avoid fresh capex and houseboat exposure until arrivals recover.
title: Srinagar Tourism, Hotels & Restaurants: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Srinagar hotel or houseboat converts room-nights into cash, and the cash arrives only when tourists physically arrive.** The asset is fixed (rooms, boats, kitchen, staff) and the cost base is largely fixed too, so a fall in arrivals hits EBITDA faster than it hits revenue. Houseboat owners on Dal Lake are the most exposed: they report being unable to meet ends for two years and some are selling boats to support families [1]. ## What has changed now
**The current signal is weak and local, not national.** Tourism bodies said the sector has been in a difficult phase since April 25 and that thousands dependent on it are under financial stress [3]. Ahead of winter, the Hoteliers Club is asking for better infrastructure, reliable essential services and aggressive promotion [2]. Peer hotel chains are posting strong growth — ITC Hotels revenue up 26 percent and EBITDA up 37 percent [4], Leela with 30% RevPAR growth [6] — but that is metro and leisure-chain demand, not Srinagar. **Do not read peer results across to a Dal Lake houseboat.**

## Where to grow
**Pursue operators with domestic, off-season and MICE-linked demand, and asset-light managers.** The Leela result was ARR-led with strong MICE demand [6]; Ventive ran 71 percent occupancy in its international leisure portfolio [5]. In Srinagar, that points to city hotels with wedding/conference and winter-event bookings, and to management-contract operators with limited capital outlay [11]. **Avoid fresh capex lending to houseboat owners and single-property seasonal hotels** until arrivals data turns; collect from customer the current occupancy, ARR and arrival numbers, since the pack gives none for Srinagar. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against cash flow, not against the building.** Take monthly occupancy and ARR certificates, monthly bank statements, and GST returns; if occupancy falls below the level you set at sanction, ask for a fresh cash-flow projection and top-up collateral. Keep tenors short and match repayment to the season. For houseboats, insist on the boat as primary collateral with a clear valuation and a personal guarantee; if the borrower cannot show two consecutive seasons of debt-service cover, decline. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch arrivals, not sentiment.** If a borrower reports falling footfall for two straight months, cut limits and move to cash-collateralised lending. If staff salaries are delayed or utility bills are unpaid, treat it as a liquidity event and inspect the property. If the borrower starts discounting room rates to fill rooms, margin is eroding — ask for the revised rate card and re-run the numbers.
watch: Two consecutive months of falling occupancy -> freeze fresh limits and seek cash collateral
Salary or utility payment delays -> inspect property and re-run cash flow
Turnover drop beyond agreed band -> ask for revised projections and top-up collateral
Arrivals below prior season -> decline fresh capex proposals
Valuation fall or boat sale enquiry -> revalue and tighten guarantee
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
